newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lamfalussy warns EU governments on jobs, deficits.
newsitem.headline: Lamfalussy warns EU governments on jobs, deficits.

text.p: European Monetary Institute (EMI) president Alexander Lamfalussy said on Tuesday that Europe was on target for monetary union in 1999, but unemployment and public sector deficits remained worrying.
"I have a great deal of confidence in progress towards monetary union," Lamfalussy told the European Parliament. "We have achieved virtual monetary stability."

But he warned that while the EMI -- the European Union's fledgling central bank -- and the national central banks were doing all they could to ensure that monetary union kicked off on time in January 1999, the bloc's 15 governments still had a lot of work to do.
Growth was strong in most EU countries, there was exchange rate stability and long-term interest rates were converging, Lamfalussy told Euro-MPs during a debate on the EMI's annual report for 1996.

But the EU was still plagued by stubbornly high unemployment rates -- now at an EU average of 11 percent and rising in Germany, France and Italy -- and excessive public sector deficits in a majority of countries, he said.
"Unemployment...remains the main challenge facing governments," Lamfalussy said.

And while public deficits were forecast to fall to under four percent this year, these improvements were due largely to tax increases and spending cuts rather than "genuine reform of our public finances and the sectors responsible for deficit -- pension, social security and health systems".
The outgoing EMI president insisted the ball was squarely in the member states' court.

"Work is well ahead in all the important areas that are the tasks of the central banks. That is true of the operational framework for monetary policy...the payments system...all the various aspects of the lives of central banks," Lamfalussy said.
"I can assure you that if there is to be a delay in (monetary union) the fact is it won't be due to the lack of preparation by central banks."

He insisted that monetary policy could help reduce unemployment that was linked to feeble economic growth, with the aid of sensible budgetary policies, but it could not affect job losses caused by structural factors.

"I think that attacking...that part of unemployment that is not a result of growth weakness means the implementation of other policies, which are structural, which involve flexibility on the labour market and policies which will bear on indirect costs of employment," the Belgian EMI chief said.
Lamfalussy said he was confident the political will was there to achieve monetary union on time.
He was speaking the day after France's new Socialist government said it would not be able to endorse the EU's budget stability pact at next week's two-day summit in Amsterdam.

EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy also insisted to parliament that there was still the political will to forge ahead with the single currency and that the Amsterdam summit would still be able to make progress.
"Amsterdam must be a success...and will be a success because no one will take the responsibility of seeing it otherwise, because no one will put the brakes on the euro," he said.
